title: Can You Trust That Medical App? IEEE’s New Registry Aims to Separate Science from Hype
summary: The app store is flooded with medical apps promising to manage everything from chronic pain to mental health. But a troubling reality lurks behind the slick interfaces: the vast majority have never been evaluated by any neutral body for safety, effectiveness, or privacy. “Patients, clinicians, payers, and health care systems often struggle to distinguish clinically meaningful therapeutic apps from those that are simply well-marketed,” says IEEE Senior Member Yuri Quintana, chair of the new IEEE Global Medical Mobile App Assessment and Registry. Launched by the IEEE Standards Association, the registry aims to fill a critical regulatory gap. Many of these apps qualify as software as a medical device (SaMD), which should be regulated by agencies like the FDA. But the explosive growth of the market has outpaced oversight. Quintana notes that some companies use deceptive advertising, implying all their apps are certified when only one is, or claiming clinical evidence that doesn’t exist. Even updated versions of previously approved apps often go unvetted. The IEEE program evaluates apps against roughly 150 consensus-based criteria across three major areas: technical soundness, ethical design, and clinical efficacy. A multidisciplinary panel of 35 experts from 10 countries—including clinicians, AI specialists, and patient advocates—developed the framework. “IEEE is uniquely positioned to create trustworthy global guardrails,” says Maria Palombini, IEEE SA’s health care lead. The registry is voluntary, but for apps that earn a listing, it offers a powerful signal of credibility. In a digital health landscape full of uncertainty, that could be a game-changer for patient safety.
why_it_matters: As teenagers increasingly turn to health apps for mental health support, fitness, or chronic condition management, this registry could become a crucial tool for making safe choices—and it shows how technology regulation must constantly evolve to protect users.

background_read: The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) is a global professional association with over 400,000 members, known for setting standards like Wi-Fi (802.11) and Bluetooth.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) normally regulates medical devices, but many health apps fall through the cracks because they are ‘general wellness’ products or the developer doesn’t seek clearance.

A notable example of an app controversy was the ‘Theranos’ effect: a health technology company falsely claimed its device could run hundreds of blood tests from a finger prick, highlighting the need for independent evaluation.
Yuri Quintana is a researcher at Harvard Medical School and expert in digital health, while Maria Palombini leads health care initiatives at IEEE SA.

Countries like Germany have already introduced ‘DiGA’ (Digital Health Applications) directories with mandatory evidence requirements, showing one regulatory approach that the IEEE registry complements on a global scale.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: A trustworthy signal for consumers and clinicians
perspectives.description: The registry could help patients and doctors quickly identify apps with real clinical evidence, reducing the risk of harmful recommendations. For ethical developers, a listing becomes a competitive advantage, potentially encouraging more companies to invest in rigorous testing and transparency.

Because the registry is voluntary, deceptive companies can simply ignore it and continue marketing unvetted apps. There is also a risk that the evaluation criteria could become a ‘rubber stamp’ if the process isn’t insulated from conflicts of interest, or that high fees could shut out small, innovative developers.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/Analytical: The challenge of regulating exponential technology
perspectives.description: This situation reflects a broader pattern where regulation lags behind software innovation—seen in social media, cryptocurrency, and AI. The IEEE’s approach mirrors industry self-regulation efforts that have both succeeded (like Wi-Fi standards) and failed when incentives aren’t aligned; its global, consensus-based model is a test case for transnational digital health governance.

The next step could be real-time monitoring of apps after listing, using AI to scan for privacy leaks or update-related changes. If successful, the IEEE model might expand to other digital tools, like AI chatbots for therapy, and could influence future FDA guidelines or even inspire a mandatory seal of approval for all health-related software.
